clinical_knowledge.topic: Stress Urinary Incontinence evaluation and management
core_concepts: Stress urinary incontinence is leakage with raised abdominal pressure; distinguish it from urgency-predominant, mixed, overflow, infection-related, and fistula-associated leakage.

Initial assessment includes a bladder diary, urinalysis, medication review, pelvic examination for atrophy/prolapse, and demonstrable cough stress test with an adequately filled bladder; measure PVR when voiding dysfunction is suspected.
Supervised pelvic-floor muscle training for at least three months, weight management when appropriate, and management of cough/constipation are first-line treatments.

Sling or other continence procedures require shared decision-making about alternatives and risks including mesh exposure/erosion, retention/voiding dysfunction, pain, infection, and need for future treatment.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: leaking urine when coughing, sneezing, or lifting heavy shopping bags

Key HPI features: 54F reports leaking small amounts of urine whenever she laughs, coughs, sneezes, or lifts heavy groceries. Has had to wear protective liners every day for 6 months. Denies painful urination.

Objective/Exam findings: Obtain urinalysis, bladder diary, pelvic examination for prolapse/atrophy, and cough stress test; measure PVR if retention, recurrent UTI, neurologic disease, or prior pelvic surgery is present.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Stress Urinary Incontinence.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Attributing continuous leakage, gross hematuria, recurrent UTI, significant prolapse, pelvic mass, pain, neurologic deficits, or elevated PVR to uncomplicated stress incontinence.
Recommending surgery without confirming the predominant type of incontinence or discussing procedural alternatives, benefits, and harms.
Using antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist drugs for exertional leakage without identifying a clinically important urgency component and reviewing retention/blood-pressure risks.
management_principles: Confirm the type and severity of leakage with history, diary, urinalysis, examination, and cough stress test; address reversible contributors.
Offer supervised pelvic-floor muscle training, lifestyle measures, continence products, and counseling before procedural care.
Refer for urogynecology/urology evaluation when symptoms are mixed/complex, PVR is elevated, prolapse or red flags are present, or she wants a procedure after informed counseling.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Has had to wear protective liners every day for 6 months. Denies painful urination.
reference_soap.objective: Use urinalysis, bladder diary, pelvic examination for atrophy/prolapse, and cough stress test; check PVR selectively for possible voiding dysfunction or complicated presentation.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Stress Urinary Incontinence.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm stress-predominant leakage and exclude infection/complicated features. Offer supervised pelvic-floor muscle training for at least three months and address weight, cough, constipation, and continence-product needs. Refer for informed procedural discussion if conservative care fails or she prefers surgery; review retention, pain, infection, and mesh-specific risks where applicable.

must_ask.say: Does the leaking happen specifically when you laugh, cough, sneeze, or lift something heavy?
Do you ever get a sudden, strong urge to urinate that you can't hold, separate from the leaking with activity?
How many vaginal deliveries have you had, and have you had any pelvic surgery before?
How many pads or liners do you need to use each day because of the leakage?
